course.title: java
course.description: A research-driven Java course from first principles through production-oriented Java 25 development. It teaches the language, object model, generics and collections, modern Java features, streams, I/O, concurrency, HTTP integration, testing, JVM internals, modules, security, diagnostics, JDBC and native interoperability. The course deliberately distinguishes Java language guarantees from implementation details and uses official Java documentation as the primary reference.
prerequisites: Ability to read simple programming logic such as variables, conditions, and loops.
A text editor or Java-capable IDE.
No prior Java experience is required.
learningOutcomes: Write, compile, run, package, document, and debug Java 25 applications.
Explain Java language semantics, object-oriented design, generics, collections, exceptions, records, sealed types, pattern matching, lambdas, and streams.
Build robust file-based and HTTP-integrating Java applications using standard APIs.
Design concurrent Java programs with executors, synchronization, atomic types, CompletableFuture, and virtual threads.
Write automated JUnit 5 tests and use Maven or Gradle for reproducible builds.
Explain JVM runtime areas, garbage collection, JIT compilation, and evidence-driven performance analysis.
Use JPMS modules, custom runtime images, Java security APIs, secure configuration, and production diagnostics appropriately.
Use JDBC safely and understand the trade-offs of reflection, method handles, and native interoperability.
Complete a realistic capstone that integrates core Java skills into a tested, packaged application.

project.explanation: The project is intentionally framework-free. The domain is immutable and validated; the service owns business operations; the repository owns persistence; the CLI owns terminal parsing; JUnit covers deterministic behavior; Maven owns the build; and JDK diagnostics are used only when evidence shows a runtime issue. The file repository writes UTF-8 text through a temporary file and replacement step so a partially written file is less likely to become the active data file. Production systems should use a transactional datastore when durability, concurrent writers, or multi-process access exceed this exercise's scope.
